choices.text: Plates jump suddenly whenever they need to move
Plates creep steadily, about two centimetres a year
Plates do not move at all

questions.feedback: That trap answer is the one to unlearn: Plates lurch in sudden jolts, snapping into new positions. Reteach point: Plates creep, they never lurch: about two centimetres a year, slower than your fingernails grow. Check scene s4: the marker creeps only a tiny distance in a whole year, so plate movement is a steady creep no one can feel.
questions.misconception: Plates lurch in sudden jolts, snapping into new positions.
questions.prompt: A pupil says plates suddenly jump into new positions. What should they say instead?

questions.answer: The Earth's crust is made of giant slabs of rock called plates.
questions.feedback: Scene s1 fixes the idea: two giant plates of rock sit apart, and together the plates make up the crust.
questions.prompt: In one sentence, say what the Earth's crust is made of.

questions.feedback: Scene s3 fixes the word: one plate slides under the other, and that sinking is called subduction.
questions.prompt: Two plates collide and one is forced down under the other. What is that sinking called?

questions.answer: The two plates collide head-on, and the denser plate is forced down and slides under the other plate.
questions.feedback: Scenes s2 and s3 fix the chain: the plates push together and collide, then the denser plate sinks underneath in subduction.
questions.prompt: In one sentence, say what happens when the two plates push together.
